title: I Posted the Group Chat Rules in the Neighborhood WhatsApp

parts.text: I muted the neighborhood WhatsApp at 11:41 p.m. and it still buzzed through the wood of my nightstand. The admin, Carol, had pinned a new rule: no street parking on game days, even with a permit. I am twenty-two, delivery driver, I see everything, I say nothing, except I had a permit. My Civic sat legally in front of my own curb. At 6:02 a.m. a printed warning appeared under my wiper, damp from dew, smelling like the cheap ink from Carol's hobby printer. "Move it or lose it - Admin." I photographed the ticket next to my permit. In the chat I wrote, "Which rule number is this?" Carol replied in thirty seconds. "Common sense. Don't make this a thing, Luis." I make deliveries for a living. I know what a thing looks like. I scrolled up to January, when Carol's son's truck blocked a hydrant during a cookout and she had written, rules are for people who don't contribute. I screenshot that too. Then I noticed the pinned message had an edit history. Before game-day parking, it had said visitors welcome, park on the street. "You're grinding coffee at war." I was. I said, "She backdated a rule onto my permit." Asha looked at the warning. "That's not even HOA letterhead." It was a Word doc with clip art of a whistle. There was a tow truck. It had Carol's cousin in the driver seat, eating a breakfast burrito, waiting for me to panic.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: Her cousin's tow truck is idling at the curb over a rule she edited at 11:39 p.m.

social.video_title: She edited the parking rule at 11:39 — Part 1/2
social.description: A WhatsApp pin, a hobby-printer warning, and a tow truck with a cousin in it. My permit was still on the dash. Would you have moved the car?

parts.text: I did not move the Civic. I walked outside in slides with the permit, the screenshot, and the edit history. The cousin, Ray, rolled down the window. Egg dripped on his hoodie. "Carol said it's a fire lane." I pointed at the hydrant, a full car-length away, and at Carol's son's usual spot, which was closer. "Call it in properly or leave," I said. He called Carol on speaker. She said, "Luis is always starting trouble." I said, "You edited the pin at 11:39. WhatsApp shows it." Ray squinted at my phone, then at the clip-art whistle. He put the truck in gear. "I don't tow fake fire lanes." Carol came out in a robe. "You are dividing the community." I posted the edit history, the hydrant photo, and her January quote in the chat with a polite caption: pinning a rule after midnight is not common sense. Twelve neighbors liked it in that cowardly WhatsApp way. Two admitted they had moved cars all season for nothing. Carol removed me as admin-adjacent, which I never was. She could not remove the screenshots. The HOA, which actually exists, emailed that game-day parking was never in the covenants. Ray waved at me now when I deliver his office sandwiches. Carol printed fewer warnings. My nightstand still buzzes, but I keep the permit in a plastic sleeve because dew wrecks ink, and I learned that the hard way from her hobby printer.

social.description: WhatsApp keeps edit history even when admins play referee. The hydrant was a full car-length away. Would you have posted the January quote?
